claim: Ras superfamily GTPase activation and inactivation occur by canonical nucleotide exchange and GTP hydrolysis mechanisms.
source: Ras superfamily GTPase activation and inactivation occur by canonical nucleotide exchange and GTP hydrolysis mechanisms.
evidence: This is a general statement about Ras superfamily GTPases that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Despite conservation of active-site residues, the Ras-related Rab GTPase activation pathway differs from Ras and between different Rabs.
source: Despite conservation of active-site residues, the Ras-related Rab GTPase activation pathway differs from Ras and between different Rabs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural and biochemical analyses presented in the manuscript comparing different Rab-GEF complexes.

claim: Analysis of DENND1-Rab35, Rabex-Rab5, TRAPP-Rab1 and DrrA-Rab1 suggests Rabs have the potential for activation by distinct GDP-release pathways.
source: Analysis of DENND1-Rab35, Rabex-Rab5, TRAPP-Rab1 and DrrA-Rab1 suggests Rabs have the potential for activation by distinct GDP-release pathways.
evidence: This claim is based on the comparative analysis of multiple Rab-GEF complexes presented in the manuscript.

claim: Conserved active-site residues in the Rab switch II region stabilising the nucleotide-free form differentiate these pathways.
source: Conserved active-site residues in the Rab switch II region stabilising the nucleotide-free form differentiate these pathways.
evidence: This is supported by the structural analysis and mutagenesis experiments showing different roles for switch II residues.

claim: For DENND1-Rab35 and DrrA-Rab1 the Rab active-site glutamine is involved in GEF mediated GDP-release.
source: For DENND1-Rab35 and DrrA-Rab1 the Rab active-site glutamine, often mutated to create constitutively active forms, is involved in GEF mediated GDP-release.
evidence: This is supported by the nucleotide exchange assays showing reduced activity with glutamine mutations (Figure 2A,B).

claim: In Rab5 the switch II aspartate is required for Rabex mediated GDP-release.
source: By contrast, in Rab5 the switch II aspartate is required for Rabex mediated GDP-release.
evidence: This is supported by the nucleotide exchange assays showing reduced activity with aspartate mutations (Figure 2C).

claim: Rab1 switch II glutamine mutants refractory to activation by DrrA can be activated by TRAPP.
source: Furthermore, Rab1 switch II glutamine mutants refractory to activation by DrrA can be activated by TRAPP, showing that a single Rab can be activated by more than one mechanistically distinct GDP-release pathway.
evidence: This is supported by the nucleotide exchange assays comparing DrrA and TRAPP activity on Rab1 mutants (Figure 2B,D).

claim: A single Rab can be activated by more than one mechanistically distinct GDP-release pathway.
source: Furthermore, Rab1 switch II glutamine mutants refractory to activation by DrrA can be activated by TRAPP, showing that a single Rab can be activated by more than one mechanistically distinct GDP-release pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of mutations on DrrA vs TRAPP mediated activation of Rab1.

claim: Rabs form an important and highly conserved subfamily of Ras-related GTPases that play essential roles in controlling membrane trafficking between the organelles of eukaryotic cells.
source: Rabs form an important and highly conserved subfamily of Ras-related GTPases that play essential roles in controlling membrane trafficking between the organelles of eukaryotic cells (Zerial and McBride, 2001; Pfeffer and Aivazian, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Specific regulators controlling nucleotide exchange and hydrolysis promote kinetic proofreading of vesicle and target organelle membrane surfaces by Rab GTPases.
source: Specific regulators controlling nucleotide exchange and hydrolysis promote kinetic proofreading of vesicle and target organelle membrane surfaces by Rab GTPases, and therefore permit accumulation of active Rabs only at the required sites (Barr and Lambright, 2010; Barr, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on Rab regulation.

claim: Mutation of the Ras switch II glutamate reduces GEF-stimulated GDP-release and compromises Ras activation.
source: Mutation of this glutamate therefore reduces GEF-stimulated GDP-release, and compromises Ras activation (Gasper et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Mutation of the conserved Rab switch II glutamate residue to alanine has little effect on the rate of GEF-mediated nucleotide exchange.
source: However, at odds with this simple idea mutation of the conserved Rab switch II glutamate residue to alanine has little effect on the rate of GEF-mediated nucleotide exchange (Gasper et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental work showing differences between Ras and Rab.

claim: In Ras the conserved switch II glutamine 61 and an arginine residue contributed by the GAP act together to promote GTP hydrolysis.
source: In Ras the conserved switch II glutamine 61 and an arginine residue contributed into the Ras active site by the GAP act together to promote GTP hydrolysis (Ahmadian et al., 1997; Scheffzek et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior structural studies of Ras-GAP complexes.

claim: The Ras switch II glutamine is frequently mutated in cancers creating a constitutively active oncogenic form of the protein.
source: This has great biological relevance since the Ras switch II glutamine is frequently mutated in cancers creating a constitutively active oncogenic form of the protein.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ras mutations in cancer.

claim: Crystal structures of Rab33 and Rab1 with TBC domain Rab GAPs reveal that the switch II glutamine does not play a direct role in GTP hydrolysis.
source: In Rabs, although the switch II glutamine is conserved, crystal structures of Rab33 and Rab1 with TBC domain Rab GAPs, Gyp1p and TBC1D20, respectively, reveal that it does not play a direct role in GTP hydrolysis (Pan et al., 2006; Gavriljuk et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies of Rab-GAP complexes.

claim: In Rab-GAP complexes, the GAP contributes both arginine and glutamine residues important for catalysis to the Rab active site.
source: Instead, the GAP contributes both arginine and glutamine residues important for catalysis to the Rab activate site (Pan et al., 2006; Gavriljuk et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: In DENND1 and DrrA complexes, the Rab P-loop lysine 21 interacts with the switch II glutamine 67 and aspartate 63 of the target GTPase.
source: In both DENND1 and DrrA complexes, the Rab P-loop lysine 21 interacts with the switch II glutamine 67 and aspartate 63 of the target GTPase (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: In the Rab1-TRAPP complex, there is no interaction of the Rab P-loop lysine with switch II residues.
source: In the case of Rab1 bound to TRAPP there is no interaction of the Rab P-loop lysine with switch II residues (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In the TRAPP complex, a glutamate at position 192 is contributed to the Rab active site by the C-terminal extension of the TRAPP Bet3 subunit.
source: Instead, a glutamate at position 192 is contributed to the Rab active site by the C-terminal extension of the TRAPP Bet3 subunit (Cai et al., 2008; Chin et al., 2009; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies and Figure 1D.

claim: For Rab21 in complex with Rabex, a conserved aspartate 74 in the switch II region interacts with the P-loop lysine 32.
source: For the Rab5 family GTPase Rab21 in complex with the Vps9 domain of the Rabex exchange factor, a conserved aspartate 74 in the switch II region of the Rab interacts with the P-loop lysine 32 (Delprato et al., 2004; Delprato and Lambright, 2007; Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies and Figure 1E.

claim: Rabex contributes an aspartate at position 313 to the Rab21 active site.
source: Analogous to TRAPP an acidic residue is also contributed by Rabex, in this case an aspartate at position 313 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Rab35 switch II glutamine 67 mutation to alanine (Q67A) greatly reduced DENND1-stimulated nucleotide exchange towards Rab35.
source: Rab35 switch II glutamine 67 mutation to alanine (Q67A) greatly reduced DENND1-stimulated nucleotide exchange towards Rab35 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by nucleotide exchange assay data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km) for DENND1-Rab35 was reduced from 2.3 × 10^4 M^-1s^-1 for wild type to ~7.5 × 10^2 M^-1s^-1 for the Q67A mutant.
source: Catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km) was reduced from 2.3 × 104 M−1s−1 similar to previous measurements using wild type Rab35 (Wu et al., 2011) to ∼7.5 × 102 M−1s−1 for the Q67A mutant.
evidence: This is quantitative data from nucleotide exchange assays.

claim: The glutamine to alanine mutation had little effect on basal GEF-independent nucleotide exchange in Rab35.
source: Importantly, the glutamine to alanine mutation had little effect on basal GEF-independent nucleotide exchange.
evidence: This is supported by the nucleotide exchange assay data.

claim: Alteration of the Rab35 switch II glutamine to glutamate (Q67E) resulted in a form that was not activated by DENND1.
source: In the case of Rab35 there is a specific requirement for glutamine at this position since alteration of the switch II glutamine to glutamate resulted in a form of Rab35 Q67E that was not activated by DENND1 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by nucleotide exchange assay data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Mutation of the Rab35 switch II glutamate 68 (E68A) had little effect on DENND1-stimulated nucleotide exchange.
source: In addition, mutation of the switch II glutamate 68 (E68A) required for nucleotide exchange in the canonical Ras activation pathway had little effect on DENND1-stimulated nucleotide exchange by Rab35 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by nucleotide exchange assay data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The Rab1 Q67A switch II mutation greatly reduced DrrA-mediated nucleotide exchange from a kcat/Km of 6.0 × 10^4 to 5.3 × 10^3 M^-1s^-1.
source: Similarly, the Q67A switch II mutation greatly reduced DrrA-mediated nucleotide exchange towards Rab1 from a kcat/Km of 6.0 × 104 to 5.3 × 103 M−1s−1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is quantitative data from nucleotide exchange assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Mutation of the Rab1 switch II glutamate (E68A) had little effect on DrrA-mediated nucleotide exchange.
source: Mutation of the switch II glutamate (E68A) in Rab1 had little effect on DrrA-mediated nucleotide exchange, kcat/Km 6.0 × 104 M−1s−1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by nucleotide exchange assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Removal of the switch II aspartate 63 resulted in increased basal release for both Rab35 and Rab1.
source: Removal of the switch II aspartate 63 contacting the P-loop lysine residue resulted in increased basal release for both Rab35 and Rab1 (Figure 2A,B), consistent with its role in nucleotide binding.
evidence: This is supported by nucleotide exchange assay data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: For DENND1, the D63A substitution resulted in a small reduction in kcat/Km to 1.7 × 10^4 M^-1s^-1.
source: For DENND1 this substitution resulted in a small reduction in kcat/Km to 1.7 × 104 M−1s−1 (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is quantitative data from nucleotide exchange assays.

claim: For DrrA, the D63A substitution increased kcat/Km over threefold to 2 × 10^5 M^-1s^-1.
source: while for DrrA kcat/Km increased over threefold to 2 × 105 M−1s−1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is quantitative data from nucleotide exchange assays.

claim: Mutation of the Rabex aspartate to alanine D313A abolished the activity of the GEF.
source: As reported previously, mutation of the Rabex aspartate to alanine D313A abolished the activity of the GEF (Figure 2C; Delprato et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by nucleotide exchange assay data and citation to prior work.

claim: Mutation of the Rab5 conserved aspartate D76A greatly reduced Rabex-mediated nucleotide exchange.
source: In support of the role of the Rab switch II aspartate in this alternative exchange pathway, mutation of the Rab5 conserved aspartate D76A greatly reduced Rabex-mediated nucleotide exchange (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by nucleotide exchange assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Catalytic efficiency for Rabex-Rab5 was reduced from 2.5×10^4 M^-1s^-1 for wild type to ~2.5 × 10^2 M^-1s^-1 for the D76A mutant.
source: Catalytic efficiency was reduced from 2.5×104 M−1s−1 in agreement with previous measurements using wild type Rab5 (Delprato et al., 2004; Delprato and Lambright, 2007) to ∼2.5 × 102 M−1s−1 for the D76A mutant.
evidence: This is quantitative data from nucleotide exchange assays.

claim: The Rab5 Q80A mutation had little effect on the activity of Rabex towards Rab5.
source: As expected from the crystal structure of the Rab21-Rabex complex (Figure 1E), the Q80A mutation (Q78 in Figure 1E) had little effect on the activity of Rabex towards Rab5 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by nucleotide exchange assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Mutation of Rab5 switch II glutamate 81 resulted in an increase in the rate of Rabex-stimulated GDP-release from a kcat/Km of 2.5 × 10^4 to 4.6 × 10^4 M^-1s^-1.
source: Interestingly, mutation of Rab5 switch II glutamate 81 (Rab21 E79 in Figure 1E) resulted in an increase in the rate of Rabex-stimulated GDP-release from a kcat/Km of 2.5 × 104 to 4.6 × 104 M−1s−1 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is quantitative data from nucleotide exchange assays.

claim: The Rab1 switch II glutamine mutation Q67A had little effect on budding yeast TRAPP activity towards Rab1/Ypt1.
source: In agreement with this idea, the switch II glutamine mutation Q67A that greatly reduced DrrA-mediated nucleotide exchange towards Rab1 (Figure 2B) had little effect on the activity of budding yeast TRAPP towards Rab1/Ypt1 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by nucleotide exchange assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Mutation of Rab1 switch II glutamate 68 increased the rate of TRAPP-stimulated GDP-release over 10-fold from a kcat/Km of 1.3 × 10^5 M^-1s^-1.
source: Interestingly, mutation of switch II glutamate 68 increased the rate of TRAPP-stimulated GDP-release over 10-fold from a kcat/Km of 1.3 × 105 M−1s−1.
evidence: This is quantitative data from nucleotide exchange assays.

claim: TRAPP complexes containing a Bet3 E192A/D193A mutant showed a fourfold reduction in GEF activity towards Rab1.
source: To confirm the requirement for the Bet3 acidic C-terminal region, TRAPP complexes containing a Bet3 E192A/D193A mutant were produced. These showed a fourfold reduction in GEF activity towards Rab1 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by nucleotide exchange assay data shown in Figure 2C (likely meant to be 2D based on context).

claim: Switch II glutamine mutation of Rab35 and Rab1 greatly reduced GTP hydrolysis stimulated by TBC1D10A and TBC1D20, respectively.
source: Switch II glutamine mutation of Rab35 and Rab1 greatly reduced GTP hydrolysis stimulated by TBC1D10A and TBC1D20, respectively, but had less than ∼1.5-fold effect on basal GTP hydrolysis (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by GTP hydrolysis assay data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The switch II glutamine mutation had no effect on the activity of RUTBC3 towards Rab5.
source: By contrast, the switch II glutamine mutation had no effect on the activity of RUTBC3 towards Rab5, but caused a greater than fivefold reduction in basal GTP hydrolysis (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by GTP hydrolysis assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The switch II glutamine mutation in Rab5 caused a greater than fivefold reduction in basal GTP hydrolysis.
source: By contrast, the switch II glutamine mutation had no effect on the activity of RUTBC3 towards Rab5, but caused a greater than fivefold reduction in basal GTP hydrolysis (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by GTP hydrolysis assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Wild type Rab35 supported delivery of Shiga toxin B cargo to the Golgi.
source: These experiments confirmed that wild type Rab35 supported delivery of cargo to the Golgi (Figure 4A, 90 min timepoint), as previously reported (Fuchs et al., 2007; Yoshimura et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by Shiga toxin uptake assay data shown in Figure 4A and citations to prior work.

claim: The switch II mutant Rab35Q67A did not actively interfere with Shiga toxin transport.
source: Under the same conditions the switch II mutant Rab35Q67A did not actively interfere with Shiga toxin transport (Figure 4A, 90 min timepoint). This indicates it does not act as a dominant negative inhibitor of transport.
evidence: This is supported by Shiga toxin uptake assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In the absence of endogenous Rab35, Rab35Q67A failed to support efficient Shiga toxin transport to the Golgi.
source: However, in the absence of the endogenous protein, Rab35Q67A failed to support efficient Shiga toxin transport to the Golgi (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by Shiga toxin uptake assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Transport efficiency was over 80% for wild type Rab35, whereas Rab35Q67A did not rescue transport above the level seen in the absence of Rab35.
source: Quantitation showed transport efficiency was over 80% for wild type Rab35, whereas Rab35Q67A did not rescue transport above the level seen in the absence of Rab35 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is quantitative data from Shiga toxin uptake assays shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Rab35 was rapidly recruited to membranes while the Rab35 Q67A or Q67L mutants showed only slow recovery in FRAP experiments.
source: In agreement with the GEF activity data, Rab35 was rapidly recruited to membranes while the Rab35 Q67A or Q67L mutants showed only slow recovery (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: For Rab5 the Q80A/L switch II mutation had no effect on the rate of recovery in FRAP experiments.
source: For Rab5 the Q80A/L switch II mutation (Q78 in Rab21, Figure 1E) did not alter activation by the GEF Rabex (Figure 2C), and accordingly had no effect on the rate of recovery (Figure 4E)
evidence: This is supported by FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: At steady state the membrane bound fractions of wild type and switch II glutamine mutant Rab35 and Rab5 were unaltered.
source: Western blot analysis confirmed that at steady state the membrane bound fractions of wild type and switch II glutamine mutant Rab35 and Rab5 were unaltered (Figure 4D,E, inset blots).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4D,E insets.

claim: Switch II glutamine mutant Rab35Q67A is defective for rapid membrane recruitment.
source: Together, these results show that switch II glutamine mutant Rab35Q67A is defective for rapid membrane recruitment, and fails to support Shiga toxin trafficking to the Golgi.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined FRAP and Shiga toxin trafficking data.

claim: DENND1 is a member of the DENN and DENN-related proteins that form the largest family of Rab nucleotide exchange factors.
source: DENND1, the Rab35 GEF studied here, is a member of the DENN and DENN-related proteins that form the largest family of Rab nucleotide exchange factors (Yoshimura et al., 2010; Barr, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: For DENN GEF targets such as Rab35, both GEF-stimulated activation and GAP-mediated inactivation are compromised by switch II glutamine mutations.
source: For DENN GEF targets such as Rab35, because both GEF-stimulated activation and GAP-mediated inactivation are compromised (Figures 2A and 3A), the Rab does not fulfil its cellular purpose (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by the combined data from Figures 2A, 3A, and 4A-C.

claim: For Rab1/Ypt1 activated by TRAPP, switch II mutants slow but do not prevent the GAP-stimulated GTPase reaction.
source: For Rab1/Ypt1 activated by TRAPP, switch II mutants slow but do not prevent the GAP-stimulated GTPase reaction (Figure 3B), possibly explaining the subcritical reduction in transport efficiency reported previously (De Antoni et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3B and citation to prior work.

claim: In Rab5, switch II glutamine Q79A mutation prolongs the lifetime of the active state by reducing the intrinsic or spontaneous rate of GTP hydrolysis.
source: In the case of Rab5, switch II glutamine Q79A mutation prolongs the lifetime of the active state by reducing the intrinsic or spontaneous rate of GTP hydrolysis (Figure 3C), and as a result promotes endosome fusion (Stenmark et al., 1994; Rybin et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3C and citations to prior work on Rab5 function.

claim: Removal of the Rab5 GAP RUTBC3 results in moderately enlarged endosomes and a delay in endocytic trafficking.
source: While removal of the Rab5 GAP RUTBC3 results in moderately enlarged endosomes and a delay in endocytic trafficking, expression of Rab5 glutamine mutants causes formation of grossly enlarged vacuolar early endosomes and blocks the pathway at this stage (Stenmark et al., 1994; Haas et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Expression of Rab5 glutamine mutants causes formation of grossly enlarged vacuolar early endosomes and blocks the endocytic pathway.
source: While removal of the Rab5 GAP RUTBC3 results in moderately enlarged endosomes and a delay in endocytic trafficking, expression of Rab5 glutamine mutants causes formation of grossly enlarged vacuolar early endosomes and blocks the pathway at this stage (Stenmark et al., 1994; Haas et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: In cells, basal hydrolysis is an important determinant of Rab5 lifetime and turnover.
source: Together these findings indicate that in cells basal hydrolysis is an important determinant of Rab5 lifetime and turnover.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of GAP removal vs glutamine mutations on Rab5 function.

claim: The major regulatory determinants of Rab5 levels at endosomal membranes are inputs driving GEF activity such as ubiquitylated cargo and PI-lipids rather than GAP activity.
source: This agrees with the idea that the major regulatory determinants of Rab5 levels at endosomal membranes are inputs driving GEF activity such as ubiquitylated cargo and PI-lipids rather than GAP activity (Del Conte-Zerial et al., 2008; Barr, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on Rab5 regulation.

claim: GAP-stimulated Rab5 turnover may occur in response to specific signals during cell migration and cell adhesion.
source: By contrast, GAP-stimulated Rab5 turnover may occur in response to specific signals during cell migration and cell adhesion (Palamidessi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on Rab5 in cell migration.

claim: Switch II glutamine mutants may generate a GTPase refractory to both GEF-mediated activation and GAP-stimulated inactivation.
source: As shown here this may generate a GTPase refractory to GEF-mediated activation and GAP-stimulated inactivation.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined biochemical and cellular data presented.

claim: Small molecule inhibitors could be developed to target mechanistically discrete Rab activation pathways and associated switch II conformations.
source: These findings raise the possibility that small molecule inhibitors could be developed to target these mechanistically discrete pathways and associated switch II conformations.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings of distinct activation pathways.

claim: The Ras-SOS GEF complex shows the Ras P-loop lysine interacting with a conserved glutamate intrinsic to the Ras active site switch II region.
source: Inspection of the Ras-SOS GEF complex shows that the Ras P-loop lysine interacts with a conserved glutamate intrinsic to the active site switch II region (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Scrutiny of DENND1-Rab35 and Rab1-DrrA Rab-GEF complex crystal structures suggests divergence from the Ras activation pathway.
source: Scrutiny of DENND1-Rab35 (Wu et al., 2011) and Rab1-DrrA (Schoebel et al., 2009; Suh et al., 2010) Rab-GEF complex crystal structures suggests divergence from the Ras activation pathway.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of crystal structures cited from prior work.

claim: Different modes of Rab P-loop interaction with the switch II region or residues from the GEF suggest distinct GDP-release pathways exist for Rab GTPases.
source: These different modes of Rab P-loop interaction with the switch II region or residues from the GEF suggest distinct GDP-release pathways exist for Rab GTPases.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural comparisons of different Rab-GEF complexes.

claim: For the first class of Rab GEFs, exemplified by DrrA and DENND1, GDP-release is promoted by interaction of the P-loop lysine with the conserved glutamine residue intrinsic to switch II.
source: For the first class of Rab GEFs, exemplified by DrrA and the DENN family member DENND1, GDP-release is promoted by interaction of the P-loop lysine with the conserved glutamine residue intrinsic to switch II (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on the structural and biochemical data presented, summarized in Figure 5A.

claim: For the second class of GEFs represented by Rabex and TRAPP, the Rab P-loop lysine interacts with a negatively charged residue provided by the GEF and extrinsic to the Rab.
source: For the second class of GEFs represented by the Vps9 family member Rabex and TRAPP, the Rab P-loop lysine interacts with a negatively charged residue, either aspartate or glutamate, provided by the GEF and extrinsic to the Rab (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on the structural and biochemical data presented, summarized in Figure 5A.

claim: Stabilisation of the P-loop lysine in Rab1 bound to TRAPP appears not to involve direct interaction with any residues in switch II.
source: This latter group can be further subdivided, since stabilisation of the P-loop lysine in Rab1 bound to TRAPP appears not to involve direct interaction with any residues in switch II.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the Rab1-TRAPP complex.

claim: For DENND1 and DrrA, the switch II glutamine of the target Rabs interacts with the P-loop lysine to promote conversion of the Rab GDP form to a nucleotide-free intermediate that then binds GTP.
source: However, for DENND1 and DrrA, the switch II glutamine of the target Rabs interacts with the P-loop lysine to promote conversion of the Rab GDP form to a nucleotide-free intermediate that then binds GTP (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on the biochemical and structural data, illustrated in Figure 5B.

claim: The switch II glutamine side chain swings from an 'in' conformation where it contacts the P-loop lysine during nucleotide exchange to an 'out' conformation where it contacts the GAP during GTP hydrolysis.
source: The glutamine side chain swings from an 'in' conformation where it contacts the P-loop lysine during nucleotide exchange (activation), to an 'out' conformation where it contacts the GAP during GTP hydrolysis (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and illustrated in Figure 5C.

claim: Rab switch II glutamine mutants will behave differently depending on the nature of their GEF activator and GAP inactivator.
source: The findings presented here also indicate that switch II glutamine mutant Rabs will behave differently depending on the nature of their GEF activator and GAP inactivator.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects observed with different Rab-GEF-GAP combinations.

claim: For Rab1/Ypt1 activated by TRAPP, switch II mutants possibly explain the subcritical reduction in transport efficiency reported previously.
source: For Rab1/Ypt1 activated by TRAPP, switch II mutants slow but do not prevent the GAP-stimulated GTPase reaction (Figure 3B), possibly explaining the subcritical reduction in transport efficiency reported previously (De Antoni et al., 2002).
evidence: This is speculation based on the biochemical data and citation to prior work.

claim: Rab5 has served as a paradigm for the function of Rab GTPases in membrane traffic.
source: Rab5 has served a paradigm for the function of Rab GTPases in membrane traffic (Zerial and McBride, 2001)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Switch II glutamine mutations in other Rabs may not behave in the same fashion as they do in Rab5.
source: yet as shown here switch II glutamine mutations in other Rabs may not behave in the same fashion as they do in Rab5.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative data on different Rabs presented in the manuscript.

claim: For Rab5 the switch II glutamine mutation results in a form that displays near wild type properties in terms of GAP-stimulated GTP hydrolysis, yet strongly compromised basal GTP hydrolysis.
source: For Rab5 the switch II glutamine mutation results in a form that displays near wild type properties in terms of GAP-stimulated GTP hydrolysis, yet strongly compromised basal GTP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is supported by the GTP hydrolysis data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: Results obtained for Rab33B and its GAP RUTBC1 show that the switch II glutamine mutation strongly compromises basal GTP hydrolysis for at least one other Rab besides Rab5.
source: Results obtained previously for Rab33B and its GAP RUTBC1 (Nottingham et al., 2011) show this is true for at least one other Rab.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on Rab33B.

claim: For Rab1 and Rab35, the switch II glutamine mutation greatly reduces GAP-stimulated GTP hydrolysis.
source: However, for Rab1 and Rab35 tested here the same mutation greatly reduces GAP-stimulated GTP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is supported by the GTP hydrolysis data presented in Figure 3A,B.
